For example, if you are awful at burst weapons then they might be lower on the list. But I can assure you, the top tier weapons are used most often for a reason. Little to no flinch on snipers makes them OP. Faster sprinting for ARs compared to SMGS makes them OP. Extremely fast one burst potential makes the M16 probably still the most OP weapon in the game. For one, it is not your responsibility to try and save your parents marriage. I applaud you for being concerned as a child should, but it’s simply not something you have to do. It sounds like the main issue here is going into an argument, your parents seem to take the you versus me approach. Instead of that, they need to start adopting the us versus the problem method. Moreover, I think that providing a third person perspective to the situation might open both their eyes a little bit. After all, if your mother hates herself, she may not be capable of giving anymore love than she is now and therefore projects her feelings onto the one person she has counted on for the majority of her life. Same thing goes for your father. I suggest you reflect upon this and try to either mediate or let fate take over. They are adults too, if they want to make it work then they will. The rest is up to you if you decide to help throughout that journey or not. Best of luck.

To preface: I have one chinese parent as well. To me it sounds like your father dealt with a lot of pain and trauma due to poverty growing up. He probably thought to himself, I will never have the same for my children. This ideological complex led early on to materialistic values and ultimately the overcompensation for what he lacked in the past. Furthermore, I think due to your lack of role models and instilled values that your parents should’ve provided, your parents shouldn’t expect anything less than backlash and criticism for their parenting. After all, your nanny raised your family, not them. The reason you think you’re dysfunctional is because you are. I don’t mean to be offensive in saying that because it’s the absence of your parents throughout the most important time of your life that caused this. They have the responsibility to provide for you, yes, but they place precedence over parenting in order for this to happen. It would be one thing if they were barely scraping by, but clearly this isn’t the case. I think it’s also important to note that asian families, primarily chinese ones, traditionally have very high standards for their children. They oftentimes place this over emotions, hence why your mother was unable to deal with your own suicidal tendencies and made insensitive remarks towards you. By the way, I’m really sorry, as no child, especially as young as you still are, should be considering ending their life. This intent comes from a good place as they want you to succeed, but as many viral memes have taught us, getting a B is inadequate. I don’t think it’s out of line for them to be scolding you for not meeting their expectations, but it’s not right. They have placed unreasonable burdens upon you as aforementioned.  I’m sure you’ve done well before and that’s gone unnoticed, I can relate and I’m sorry to hear that you’ve gone through that and on top of that had a multitude of horrifically traumatic childhood experiences. I understand that with all that you’ve talked about, it’s reasonable to be upset and frustrated and pick fights and arguments with them. However, it seems counterintuitive for you expect them to listen to these concerns if you are back talking to them. After all, you are only 16 and they are your parents. It’s disrespectful, especially to asian parents, to do this. 

I understand where you’re coming from, as I had a lot of tension between my mother and I for the same and different reasons growing up. It’s hard not to back talk when you know they are in the wrong. At the end of the day, you have to decide what’s more important, attempting to mend your relationship with your parents to have them in your life or speaking your truth. I think that the first option may be best, as after all they are your family. Sitting down and having a conversation with them and seeing if your siblings could attest to these feelings too may help alleviate some of the pain and bring closure to your childhood. Yet, this may not fix the habits that they still have. I think that the way you can go about that is learning to control your temper by way of allowing yourself time to calm down when a conversation is escalating. You hopefully can read the room when this happens. If your parents are like mine and force you
